The short answer

GPS is a space-based radio-navigation system owned by the U.S. Government and operated by the U.S. Air Force. NASA describes it as able to pinpoint a three-dimensional position to meter-level accuracy, and time to the 10-nanosecond level, anywhere in the world at any hour [1]. The core idea is that each satellite transmits its own position and the time, and a receiver works out where it is by calculating how long those signals took to arrive [1]. NOAA uses a helpful comparison: the signals act like a giant tape measure stretched between the receiver and each satellite [2].

Three parts, one system

NASA divides GPS into three segments [1].

The space segment is the constellation of satellites. NASA says there are at least 24 of them, spread over six orbital planes tilted 55 degrees from the equator, in medium Earth orbit at about 20,200 kilometers (12,550 miles), and each circles the planet roughly every 12 hours. Today the constellation has more than 30 operational satellites, each carrying redundant atomic clocks [1]. The FAA's page counts 31 satellites, which is consistent with that more-than-30 figure, although it gives the altitude as approximately 11,000 miles [3]. The two figures are presented differently, and the more specific kilometer and mile values from NASA and NOAA are the ones used in this article [1][2]. For a general reader the takeaway is simply that the satellites are far higher than airplanes and far lower than the geostationary satellites used for television.

The control segment is a network of stations on the ground that monitor and maintain the satellites [1]. NOAA adds that these ground stations help determine where each satellite was and where it is forecast to be [2]. That matters because a receiver can only trust the position a satellite reports if the position was calculated accurately.

The user segment is everything that receives the signals: the chip in a phone, a car navigation unit, a surveying instrument, or a flight computer [1]. Because receivers only listen, an unlimited number of them can work at once without adding load to the satellites. This is one of the reasons GPS spread so widely.

How a receiver finds you

NOAA explains that satellites act like stars in a constellation: we know where they are supposed to be at any given time [2]. Each satellite broadcasts its position and the time at regular intervals, and the receiver notes when each signal arrives. Radio waves travel at a known speed, so the delay between sending and receiving translates into a distance. Once the receiver has calculated its distance from four or more satellites, NOAA says, it knows where you are [2].

It is worth pausing on why four, since the sources state the number without fully explaining it. This part is a general explanation of satellite geometry rather than a claim from the cited pages. A distance from one satellite places you somewhere on a sphere around it. A second distance narrows that to a circle where two spheres intersect, and a third narrows it to two points, one of which is usually far out in space. That would suffice if the receiver had a perfect clock. In practice a phone has an inexpensive clock that is far less precise than the atomic clocks on the satellites, and a tiny timing error becomes a large distance error, because radio waves cover about 300,000 kilometers every second. The fourth satellite lets the receiver solve for its own clock error as well as for its three position coordinates. NOAA also notes that the satellites are arranged so that users can view at least four of them from virtually any point on the planet [2].

A useful side effect is that GPS is also a timing system. Because a receiver ends up with a very accurate time, many systems use GPS to synchronize clocks. NASA notes that GPS can provide accurate time synchronization, and that its timing capability can reduce a spacecraft's need for expensive on-board clocks [1].

Where the idea came from

NASA traces the origin to the Sputnik era. Scientists tracked the first satellite by the shift in its radio signal known as the Doppler effect, which became the foundational idea for modern GPS [1]. In the early 1970s, the Department of Defense wanted a robust and stable satellite navigation system, drew on earlier work by Navy scientists, and launched its first NAVSTAR satellite in 1978. The 24-satellite system became fully operational in 1993 [1]. The FAA gives a slightly different framing of the start date: the Navstar Global Positioning System was initiated in 1973 as a joint civil and military technical program that combined strengths of earlier efforts named TRANSIT, TIMATION, and Project 621B [3]. Read together, 1973 marks the start of the program, 1978 the first satellite launch, and 1993 the point at which the full constellation was working.

How accurate is GPS, really?

There are two different answers, and they are both correct. NASA states that, per the published performance standards, GPS provides a 95 percent accuracy of approximately 10 meters horizontally and 20 meters vertically. It then adds that actual performance can be much better depending on the scenario, and that the global average ranging error of the signal in space has been demonstrated to be as small as one meter or better in recent years [1]. NOAA's consumer-oriented wording is that a position can often be determined within a few yards, while many high-tech receivers can find it to within a fraction of an inch [2].

The difference between a few meters and a fraction of an inch comes largely from the equipment and method. A phone listens to one civilian signal and has to guess at some of the delays the signal experienced on the way. Professional receivers use more careful techniques and, as NOAA describes, can draw on a nationwide network of permanent GPS stations called Continuously Operating Reference Stations, which NOAA's National Geodetic Survey uses to monitor the movement of Earth's surface and to provide positioning products for surveying, construction, navigation, and mapping [2].

Two caveats follow from this. First, the published figures are statements about a typical receiver under standard conditions, not guarantees for any particular moment. Second, the sources do not discuss every environmental effect. A reader should not assume the numbers apply equally in a dense city, indoors, or in a canyon, where buildings and terrain can block or reflect signals. That is a general expectation and was not examined in the sources above.

Who can use it

NASA says GPS offers two levels of service. The Standard Positioning Service is available to all users continuously and worldwide, free of any direct user charges. The Precise Positioning Service uses a different code on two frequencies and is restricted to the U.S. armed forces, federal agencies, and selected allied armed forces and governments [1]. The consumer navigation on a phone relies on the standard service.

The FAA's page also clarifies who is responsible for what. The Department of Defense operates and maintains GPS, an executive committee on space-based positioning, navigation, and timing guides the department on matters affecting federal agencies, the Coast Guard acts as the civil interface for the public, and the FAA oversees the use of GPS in civil aviation [3]. If you ever want to report a problem with GPS service, that division of roles tells you where such reports are directed.

Beyond maps

GPS is more than turn-by-turn directions. NASA says it is used as a remote-sensing tool to support atmospheric and ionospheric sciences, geodesy and geodynamics, from monitoring sea levels and ice melt to measuring the Earth's gravity field [1]. Spacecraft can also use it: GPS-based navigation lets a satellite compute its own trajectory on board, which NASA says increases autonomy and reduces the burden on tracking stations, although most missions still rely mainly on tracking through communication channels [1]. The FAA notes that GPS is used in a wide variety of applications around the world because its capabilities are accessible with small, inexpensive equipment [3].

Common misunderstandings

One misunderstanding is that your phone transmits to GPS satellites. According to the descriptions above, receivers process signals that satellites broadcast; the GPS satellites transmit and receivers listen [1]. Any sharing of your location with a map app comes from the app and your phone's network connection, not from the satellites themselves. A second is that GPS needs the internet. The system itself does not; the sources describe a radio-navigation system with no network requirement, although phones often use cellular data to get a faster first fix or to download maps, which is a general observation outside the cited pages. A third is that GPS is the only satellite navigation system. NASA refers to GPS as one of several Global Navigation Satellite Systems and mentions Russia's GLONASS as another [1].

What to remember

GPS works because a few facts line up: satellites know where they are, they broadcast the time on very precise clocks, radio travels at a known speed, and a receiver can turn the delay of four or more signals into a position and a corrected clock. The headline accuracy is a few meters for ordinary users, better in good conditions and with specialized equipment, and the whole system rests on one-way broadcasts rather than any two-way tracking. When your map dot drifts or jumps, it helps to remember that it is an estimate built from timing measurements, and that the quality of the estimate depends on what your receiver can hear.

Sources

[1] NASA, Global Positioning System (GPS) - https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/somd/space-communications-navigation-program/gps/

[2] NOAA National Ocean Service, What is GPS? - https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/gps.html

[3] Federal Aviation Administration, Satellite Navigation - Global Positioning System (GPS) - https://www.faa.gov/about/office_org/headquarters_offices/ato/service_units/techops/navservices/gnss/gps

title: GDP Explained: What It Measures and What It Leaves Out
summary: GDP explained in plain terms: what gross domestic product counts, how real and nominal GDP differ, why estimates get revised, and what the number misses.
seo: what is GDP, gross domestic product explained, real vs nominal GDP, GDP limitations
author: knowledge blog
content:
Few numbers in the news carry as much weight as gross domestic product. Headlines say the economy grew at an annual rate of some percentage, analysts argue about whether it signals a slowdown, and governments cite it when setting policy. Yet the definition behind the number is easy to skim past. This guide explains what GDP counts, how the real and nominal versions differ, why the first estimate is later revised, how countries are compared, and what the figure does not tell you. It draws on explanations from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis and the International Monetary Fund, and it does not offer investment or financial advice.

The core definition

The Bureau of Economic Analysis, or BEA, defines gross domestic product as the value of the final goods and services produced in the United States [1]. The IMF's Finance and Development magazine gives a very similar definition for any country: the monetary value of final goods and services produced in a country in a given period of time, such as a quarter or a year [2].

Three words in that definition do most of the work. Final means that the value of intermediate inputs is not counted a second time. The flour that goes into a loaf of bread is not added on top of the bread. Produced means that GDP measures output, not wealth or savings. Domestic means that it counts what is made inside a country's borders. The IMF's author, Tim Callen, contrasts it with gross national product, which counts the output of a country's residents wherever they work. His example is that the output of a German-owned factory in the United States is included in U.S. GDP but in German gross national product [2].

What is included and what is not

According to the IMF article, GDP includes goods and services produced for sale in the market, plus some nonmarket production, such as defense or education services provided by the government. It excludes unpaid work, such as household work or volunteer services, and black-market activities [2]. That has a practical consequence. If a family member cares for a child at home, the work does not appear in GDP; if the family pays a care provider, the same work does. A rise in measured output can therefore partly reflect activity moving from the unpaid to the paid sector, a general implication of the definition rather than a claim made in either source.

The word gross also matters. The IMF explains that gross does not subtract depreciation, meaning the wear and tear on capital stock, and that subtracting depreciation gives net domestic product [2].

Three ways to add it up

The IMF describes three theoretical approaches that, in principle, should arrive at the same total [2].

The production approach sums value added at each stage of production, where value added is total sales less the value of intermediate inputs. The expenditure approach adds purchases by final users: household consumption, business investment, government purchases, and foreigners. The income approach sums the incomes generated by production, namely compensation of employees and the operating surplus of companies [2].

It is useful to think of these as three views of the same flow of activity. Money spent on a final product is also income to the people who made it. In practice statistical agencies use many data sources and the approaches rarely match perfectly, which is one reason estimates can change. The BEA says GDP is the signature piece of its National Income and Product Accounts, which measure the value and makeup of the nation's output, the types of income generated, and how that income is used [1].

Real versus nominal GDP

The figure most people hear is not a dollar amount but a percentage. The BEA says that the number commonly called GDP is the rate of change in real GDP from the previous quarter or year [1]. Real, or chained, GDP has been adjusted to remove the effects of inflation over time so that different periods can be compared. Current-dollar, or nominal, GDP is based on market prices during the period being measured [1]. The IMF says the same thing in other words: nominal GDP is collected at current prices and, to compare periods, it is converted to constant prices using a price deflator [2].

Here is why the distinction matters. Suppose nominal output rises 5 percent while prices rise 3 percent. The numbers in this example are invented to illustrate the idea and are not data from either source. Real growth is roughly 2 percent, because most of the increase merely reflects higher prices. A headline that quoted the nominal figure alone would overstate how much more was actually produced. For that reason, when a news story says the economy grew, the real figure is almost always the one being reported.

Seasonal adjustment and annual rates

Two more conventions affect how to read quarterly numbers. The BEA seasonally adjusts GDP data to remove the effects of yearly patterns, such as winter weather, holidays, or factory production schedules, so that remaining movements better reflect real patterns in economic activity. It also publishes data that are not seasonally adjusted [1]. In addition, quarterly GDP data are reported at annual rates for ease of comparison, unless otherwise specified [1]. An annual rate expresses what the growth would be if the quarter's pace continued for a full year, so a quarterly figure of 2 percent at an annual rate does not mean the economy grew 2 percent in those three months.

Why the numbers get revised

The BEA estimates GDP for each quarter three times. The advance estimate comes about a month after the quarter ends and is an early look based on the best information then available. The second and third estimates incorporate additional source data that were not available the month before, improving accuracy [1]. The practical lesson is that a first reading is provisional. If the advance number for a quarter differs a little from the later one, that does not mean someone made an error; it means more data arrived. The BEA also offers an explainer for readers curious about why old GDP numbers change, which indicates how common the question is [1].

What people use it for

The BEA lists several uses. It helps answer how fast the economy is growing, how one state's economy compares with others, and which industries are growing or slowing. The White House and Congress use it to plan spending and tax policy, the Federal Reserve uses it when setting monetary policy, and state and local governments and businesses rely on it as well [1]. The BEA also publishes GDP by state, county, territory, and industry, so the concept scales to smaller areas [1].

The IMF article adds a link to jobs. When real GDP is growing strongly, employment is likely to increase, and when GDP is shrinking, employment often declines. Growth can be too weak to create enough jobs even when it is positive. Real GDP growth moves in cycles of booms and slower periods, and a recession is often defined as two consecutive quarters of falling output [2]. The IMF notes that in the United States there were six recessions of varying length and severity between 1950 and 2011, and that the National Bureau of Economic Research is the body that determines U.S. business cycle dates [2]. The two-quarter rule is therefore a common rule of thumb rather than the official method in the United States.

Comparing countries

GDP is measured in each country's own currency, so comparisons need a common currency, usually the U.S. dollar. The IMF describes two ways to convert. Market exchange rates use the rates in the foreign exchange market. Purchasing power parity, or PPP, rates use the rate at which one currency would have to be converted to buy the same basket of goods and services in each country [2]. Callen explains that non-traded goods and services such as haircuts tend to be cheaper in lower-income countries, so for most emerging market and developing countries the ratio between the market and PPP exchange rates is between 2 and 4, and using PPP typically gives them a higher dollar GDP. For advanced economies the two rates tend to be much closer [2]. When you see a ranking of the largest economies, it is worth checking which method it used, as the order can change.

What GDP does not tell you

The IMF is direct about the limits: GDP is not a measure of overall standard of living or well-being. It omits or captures poorly such factors as environmental damage and other external costs, depletion of nonrenewable natural resources, changes in leisure time, and how output is distributed among residents [2]. The article mentions alternatives and supplements, including the United Nations Human Development Index, which combines GDP per capita with life expectancy, literacy, and school enrollment, as well as the Genuine Progress Indicator and the Gross National Happiness Index, and it notes that each has critics [2].

This balance is worth keeping in mind. GDP is useful because it is consistent, regularly published, and built on international standards. The IMF notes that national statistical agencies compile it following established international standards, set out in the System of National Accounts [2]. It is a poor choice as a measure of happiness or sustainability because it was not designed for those purposes.

How to read a GDP headline

A few habits help. Check whether the figure is real or nominal. Note whether it is an annual rate and whether it is an advance, second, or third estimate. Remember that a positive number can still be weak and a negative quarter is not automatically an official recession. And when someone uses GDP to argue that people are better or worse off, ask what GDP leaves out, such as unpaid work, environmental costs, and who receives the income.

Conclusion

GDP is best understood as a carefully built accounting total of what an economy produces and sells to final users, adjusted for inflation and the calendar so that periods can be compared. It is a valuable gauge of economic activity and a poor gauge of well-being. Reading it with its definitions, revisions, and limitations in mind turns a single headline percentage into a more reliable piece of information.

Sources

[1] U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, What to Know About GDP - https://www.bea.gov/resources/learning-center/what-to-know-gdp

[2] International Monetary Fund, Finance and Development, Gross Domestic Product: An Economy's All (Tim Callen, 2019) - https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/fandd/issues/Series/Back-to-Basics/gross-domestic-product-GDP

title: How to Wash Your Hands Properly: CDC and WHO Guidance
summary: How to wash your hands properly: the five CDC steps, key times to wash, when sanitizer helps, and what WHO evidence says about hand hygiene and infections.
seo: how to wash your hands properly, handwashing steps, hand sanitizer vs soap, hand hygiene
author: knowledge blog
content:
Handwashing is one of the most familiar health habits and one of the least carefully practiced. Most people rinse for a few seconds and move on. Public health agencies keep repeating the advice because the habit is cheap, available almost everywhere, and tied to the spread of common illnesses. This article explains how to wash your hands properly according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, when soap and water are the better choice than sanitizer, and what the World Health Organization says about hand hygiene in health care. It is general public health information, not personal medical advice; anyone with a skin condition or a health concern should ask a clinician.

Why handwashing matters

The CDC says that washing hands can keep you healthy and prevent the spread of respiratory and diarrheal infections, and that many diseases and conditions are spread by not washing hands with soap and clean running water [1]. It describes how germs spread from person to person or from surfaces to people. You can pick them up or pass them on when you touch your eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands, prepare or eat food and drinks with unwashed hands, touch contaminated surfaces or objects, or blow your nose, cough, or sneeze into your hands and then touch other people's hands or common objects [1].

Notice that the habit protects in two directions. Washing reduces the chance you carry germs to your own face, and it reduces the chance you leave them on door handles, food, or someone else's hands. That second benefit is why the advice is described as a way to protect your loved ones as well as yourself [1].

The five steps

The CDC gives a five-step routine to follow every time [1].

Wet your hands with clean, running water, which can be warm or cold, turn off the tap, and apply soap. Lather by rubbing your hands together with the soap, including the backs of your hands, between your fingers, and under your nails. Scrub for at least 20 seconds. The CDC suggests humming the Happy Birthday song from beginning to end twice if you need a timer. Rinse well under clean, running water. Dry with a clean towel or an air dryer [1].

A few of these details are easy to miss. The instruction is to turn off the tap after wetting, which means you do not need to keep the water running while you scrub. The scrub time is a minimum, not a target. And the areas people skip, such as the backs of the hands, the spaces between fingers, and the area under the nails, are explicitly named, so a quick rub of the palms is not the full routine [1].

When to wash

The CDC lists key times when you are likely to get and spread germs [1]. They include before, during, and after preparing food; before and after eating; before and after caring for someone at home who is sick with vomiting or diarrhea; before and after treating a cut or wound; after using the toilet; after changing diapers or cleaning up a child who has used the toilet; after blowing your nose, coughing, or sneezing; after touching an animal, animal feed, or animal waste; after handling pet food or treats; and after touching garbage [1].

If that list feels long, a practical way to use it is to link washing to events that already happen in your day, such as arriving home, finishing in the kitchen, or leaving the bathroom. This tip is a general habit-building suggestion rather than something stated in the cited guidance.

When sanitizer is acceptable

Soap and water are not always at hand. The CDC says that if they are not readily available, you can use a hand sanitizer containing at least 60 percent alcohol, and that you can check the product label to confirm it [1][2]. Its separate sanitizer guidance recommends applying the product to the palm of one hand, covering all surfaces of both hands, and rubbing until the hands are dry, which should take around 20 seconds. It tells users not to rinse or wipe off the sanitizer before it is dry because it may not work well [2].

The CDC is clear that sanitizer is a second choice in many situations. Soap and water remove all types of germs from hands, while sanitizer acts by killing certain germs on the skin. Sanitizers can quickly reduce the number of germs in many situations, but they do not get rid of all types of germs and may be less effective when hands are visibly dirty or greasy. They might not remove harmful chemicals such as pesticides or heavy metals like lead, and soap and water are more effective at removing certain germs, such as norovirus, Cryptosporidium, and Clostridioides difficile, as well as chemicals [2].

That leads to a simple rule. After gardening, camping, fishing, or any activity that leaves your hands visibly dirty or greasy, the CDC advises washing with soap and water when a handwashing station is available [2]. The CDC also notes that children should be supervised when they use alcohol-based sanitizer, especially in schools and childcare facilities, to prevent swallowing alcohol [2].

What WHO adds: the health care evidence

The World Health Organization approaches hand hygiene from the angle of health care facilities, but its evidence helps explain why public health agencies emphasize the practice. WHO reports that, according to available evidence, compliance with hand hygiene recommendations during health care remains suboptimal around the world, with an average of 59.6 percent compliance in intensive care units up to 2018, and extreme differences between high-income and low-income countries, at 64.5 percent versus 9.1 percent [3].

It also reports that out of every 100 patients in acute-care hospitals, seven patients in high-income countries and 15 in low- and middle-income countries will acquire at least one health care-associated infection during their hospital stay [3]. WHO says that most of these infections are preventable through hand hygiene performed at the right times, and that hand hygiene improvement programs can prevent up to 50 percent of avoidable infections acquired during health care delivery, with economic savings on average 16 times the cost of implementation [3].

These numbers describe health care settings, with trained staff and specific protocols, so they should not be treated as a prediction of how much risk reduction an individual will get at home. What they do show is that even in settings where the stakes are obvious, the habit is hard to maintain, and that systematic reminders and training raise adherence [3]. WHO also notes that medical gloves are crucial for preventing infection when exposed to blood and body fluids, but they do not replace proper hand hygiene [3].

A practical home routine

Putting the guidance together, a sensible routine looks like this. Keep soap at every sink you use, including the kitchen. Wash at the key moments the CDC lists, especially before eating or handling food and after the toilet. Take the full 20 seconds, covering the backs of hands, between the fingers, and under the nails. Dry with a clean towel or an air dryer. Carry a sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol for situations where there is no sink, and switch to soap and water when your hands are dirty or greasy. Everything in that list comes from the CDC and WHO guidance, apart from the practical ideas about where to keep soap and sanitizer, which are simply sensible applications [1][2][3].

Common questions

Does the water have to be hot? The CDC says warm or cold clean water is fine [1]. Is antibacterial soap required? The CDC pages cited here do not say that it is, and they describe ordinary soap with scrubbing as the standard method [1]. Is sanitizer as good as washing? In many situations it is a reasonable substitute, but the CDC ranks soap and water as the best way to get rid of germs in most situations and notes the exceptions above [1][2]. Is a quick rinse enough? The CDC guidance specifies lathering and scrubbing for at least 20 seconds, so a rinse alone is not what is recommended [1].

Conclusion

Proper handwashing is a short sequence of small choices: wet, lather, scrub for 20 seconds, rinse, and dry, done at the moments when germs are most likely to move. Sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol is a useful backup when soap is unavailable, but it does not replace washing when hands are dirty. WHO's evidence from hospitals shows how much difference the habit can make and how often it is missed. The advice is not complicated, and its value comes from doing it consistently.

Sources

[1] Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, About Handwashing - https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/about/index.html

[2] Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Hand Sanitizer Guidelines and Recommendations - https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/about/hand-sanitizer.html

[3] World Health Organization, Hand hygiene - https://www.who.int/teams/integrated-health-services/infection-prevention-control/hand-hygiene

title: Why Is the Sky Blue? Rayleigh Scattering Explained
summary: Why is the sky blue? Learn how air molecules scatter sunlight, why the sky is not violet, why sunsets turn red, and why clouds look white.
seo: why is the sky blue, Rayleigh scattering, why sunsets are red, why the sky is not violet
author: knowledge blog
content:
A clear daytime sky looks blue, a sunset looks orange or red, and a cloud looks white. All three observations come from the same sunlight passing through the same atmosphere, yet the colors differ. This article answers the question many people ask as children and rarely revisit: why is the sky blue? It explains the physics in plain language, covers the common follow-up questions about violet light and sunsets, and points out where popular explanations go wrong.

The short answer

NASA's educational site gives a compact version: sunlight reaches Earth's atmosphere and is scattered in all directions by the gases and particles in the air, and blue light is scattered more than other colors because it travels as shorter, smaller waves [1]. The University of California Riverside physics FAQ, written by Philip Gibbs, puts it in similar terms: a clear, cloudless daytime sky is blue because molecules in the air scatter blue light from the Sun more than they scatter red light [2]. Everything else in this article is a refinement of that statement.

Sunlight is a mixture of colors

The Sun's light looks white, but it is a blend of all the colors of the rainbow. NASA points to the familiar prism experiment, in which white light passing through a prism separates into its colors [1]. The FAQ credits Isaac Newton with demonstrating this and explains that colors are distinguished by wavelength. The visible spectrum runs from red light at roughly 720 nanometres to violet at roughly 380 nanometres, with orange, yellow, green, blue, and indigo in between [2].

NASA describes light as traveling in waves, some short and choppy and some long and lazy, with blue waves shorter than red waves [1]. That difference in wavelength is the whole story, because scattering is sensitive to it.

What scattering means

Light travels in a straight line unless something interferes. NASA lists three possibilities: it can be reflected, like light from a mirror; bent, like light passing through a prism; or scattered, like light meeting the molecules of the gases in the atmosphere [1]. Scattering sends light off in new directions. When you look at a patch of sky away from the Sun, the light reaching your eye is sunlight that was redirected toward you by the air.

The HyperPhysics site from Georgia State University, authored by R. Nave, names this process Rayleigh scattering. It is more effective at short wavelengths, so the light scattered down to Earth at a large angle from the direction of the Sun is predominantly at the blue end of the spectrum [3]. HyperPhysics adds that Rayleigh scattering applies to scattering from molecules and from particles up to about a tenth of the wavelength of the light [3].

A history of getting the explanation right

The physics FAQ tells a story that corrects a widespread belief. John Tyndall took early steps in 1859 by showing that when light passes through a clear fluid holding small particles in suspension, shorter blue wavelengths are scattered more strongly than red. You can see a version of this with a beam of white light through a tank of water with a little milk or soap mixed in: from the side the beam looks bluish, while light seen from the end looks reddened [2].

Lord Rayleigh studied the effect in more detail a few years later and showed that, for sufficiently small particles, the amount of light scattered is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength. The FAQ calculates that blue light is therefore scattered roughly ten times more than red light [2]. That ratio is an approximation based on the wavelengths 700 and 400 nanometres, not a precise measurement of the sky.

Tyndall and Rayleigh assumed that dust and water droplets were responsible. The FAQ notes that people still sometimes say this, but later scientists realised that if it were true, sky color would vary with humidity and haze far more than it does. They concluded that molecules of oxygen and nitrogen are enough, and Einstein settled the matter in 1911 by calculating the scattering from molecules in detail, a result that agreed with experiment [2]. So the common answer that dust makes the sky blue is a myth; air itself does the job.

Why the sky is not violet

If shorter wavelengths scatter most strongly, a careful reader will ask why the sky is not violet, since violet has the shortest visible wavelength. The FAQ offers two parts to the answer. First, the Sun's emission is not equal at all wavelengths, and the upper atmosphere absorbs some of it, so there is less violet in the light that reaches the lower atmosphere. Second, our vision matters: our eyes are less sensitive to violet [2].

The FAQ describes the three types of cone cells in the retina, which respond most strongly to red, green, and blue wavelengths, and notes that colors are constructed by the visual system from the proportions in which the cones are stimulated. Scattered indigo and violet light also stimulates the red cones slightly, which gives it a blue appearance with a hint of red. When the signals are combined, red and green cones are stimulated about equally and blue more strongly, producing the pale blue we see [2]. In other words, the color of the sky is partly a property of the light and partly a property of the observer. The FAQ also suggests it may not be a coincidence that our vision sees the sky as a pure hue, although it presents this as a possibility rather than a proven conclusion [2].

Why the sky fades toward the horizon

Look near the horizon and the sky is lighter, sometimes almost white. NASA explains that sunlight reaching you from low in the sky has passed through more air than sunlight arriving from directly overhead. The air molecules have scattered and re-scattered the blue light many times in many directions, and the surface of Earth also reflects and scatters light. All this scattering mixes the colors together again, so we see more white and less blue [1].

HyperPhysics describes a related observation. The blue of the sky is more saturated when you look further from the Sun, and the nearly white scattering near the Sun comes from Mie scattering, which is not strongly wavelength dependent [3]. The site's own measurements of a sky photograph show red and green increasing as a fraction of blue toward the Sun, meaning the color is becoming less saturated. The author warns that these data are qualitative only, since the photo had been transformed several times and the monitor was not calibrated [3].

Why sunsets are red

As the Sun sinks, its light must cross more of the atmosphere to reach you. NASA says that even more of the blue light is scattered away, allowing reds and yellows to pass straight through to your eyes. It adds that small particles of dust, pollution, or other aerosols also scatter blue light, leaving more purely red and yellow light to go through the atmosphere [1].

The physics FAQ gives a useful nuance: when the air is clear, a sunset appears yellow, because some of the blue has been scattered away. When the air contains many small particles, natural or otherwise, the sunset is more red. Sunsets over the sea may look orange because of salt particles in the air. The FAQ also notes that blue light is more likely to be scattered twice or more over long paths, which leaves the yellow, red, and orange colors [2]. So the vivid sunsets people admire often depend on what is in the air, not only on the geometry of the Sun.

Why clouds are white

Clouds do not share the sky's blue. HyperPhysics explains that the water droplets in clouds are much larger than air molecules, and their scattering is almost independent of wavelength across the visible range, so clouds appear white to achromatic gray [3]. The FAQ makes the same point about clouds and dust haze: particles larger than the wavelength of light scatter all wavelengths about equally, which is called Mie scattering [2]. HyperPhysics adds that the same effect explains the white light from mist and fog [3].

The pattern is useful as a rule of thumb. Very small scatterers, such as air molecules, favor blue. Scatterers comparable to or larger than the wavelength of light, such as cloud droplets, favor no color in particular and look white. That rule of thumb is a summary drawn from the sources, not a precise statement of the full theory.

Other blue skies and other colors

The same ideas explain more unusual cases. The FAQ notes that some mountainous regions are known for a blue haze, which it attributes to aerosols of terpenes from vegetation reacting with ozone to form particles of about 200 nanometres, which scatter blue light. It also says a forest fire or volcanic eruption may sometimes fill the air with particles of 500 to 800 nanometres, the right size to scatter red light, which can give the Moon a blue tinge [2]. Not all blue in nature is scattering, however. The FAQ points out that water absorbs longer wavelengths over distances greater than about 20 metres, so light under the sea is blue for a different reason [2].

On other worlds the results differ. NASA says the answer depends on what is in the atmosphere. Mars has a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide and filled with fine dust, which scatters light differently from Earth's air. NASA reports that images from its landers show an orange or reddish daytime Martian sky and a blue-gray tone around the Sun at sunset, the opposite of what happens on Earth [1].

Common misconceptions

The sky is not blue because it reflects the ocean. The FAQ says the reverse is partly true: the sea can look blue from the beach because it reflects the sky [2]. The sky is not blue because of dust. As described above, the molecules of the air are enough [2]. The sky is not simply violet because violet scatters most. The Sun's output, atmospheric absorption, and human vision all shape the result [2]. And blue light is not the only color scattered; all colors scatter, but blue does so more strongly [1].

Try it yourself

The milk-in-water demonstration described by the FAQ is a safe way to see scattering in action. Add a little milk or a few drops of liquid soap to a clear tank of water and shine a white flashlight through it in a dim room. Looking from the side, the beam looks bluish; looking at the beam end-on, it appears more orange or reddish [2]. The exact colors depend on how much milk you add, so treat this as an observation rather than a measurement. You can also look away from the Sun on a clear day and compare the deep blue overhead with the paler color near the horizon, an observation that matches the descriptions from NASA and HyperPhysics [1][3]. Never look directly at the Sun.

Conclusion

The sky is blue because air molecules scatter short wavelengths of sunlight more strongly than long ones, and our eyes combine the scattered light into a pale blue. The same principle explains the paler horizon, the reds of sunset, and the white of clouds, once you account for the distance light travels and the size of the particles it meets. The most common popular explanations, such as dust, ocean reflection, or the simple claim that blue is the shortest wavelength, leave out part of the answer. The better account combines physics, atmospheric composition, and human vision.

Sources

[1] NASA Space Place, Why Is the Sky Blue? - https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/blue-sky/en/

[2] Philip Gibbs, Why is the sky blue? (Physics FAQ, University of California, Riverside) - https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/physics/General/BlueSky/blue_sky.html

[3] R. Nave, Blue Sky (HyperPhysics, Georgia State University) - http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/atmos/blusky.html

title: The Marshall Plan Explained: Why the US Aided Europe
summary: The Marshall Plan explained: why the US offered postwar aid to Europe, what the 1948 law said, how much Congress approved, and where historians still disagree.
seo: Marshall Plan explained, European Recovery Program, Marshall speech 1947, Economic Cooperation Act of 1948
author: knowledge blog
content:
In the spring of 1948 the United States committed billions of dollars to rebuild countries that had been enemies, allies, and battlegrounds only three years earlier. The program became known as the Marshall Plan, and it remains one of the most cited examples of foreign aid in modern history. This article explains the Marshall Plan using two public sources from the US government: the State Department's historical summary and the National Archives' milestone document page, which includes the text of Secretary of State George Marshall's 1947 speech and part of the 1948 law. It covers the problem Marshall described, how the program was designed, what Congress approved, and which questions remain open.

Europe after the war

The National Archives page sets the scene starkly. When World War II ended in 1945, Europe lay in ruins: cities were shattered, economies devastated, and people faced famine. In the two years that followed, the Soviet Union's control of Eastern Europe and the vulnerability of Western European countries to Soviet expansion heightened the sense of crisis [2]. The State Department similarly says that Europe remained ravaged by war and, in the American view of the time, susceptible to exploitation by internal and external Communist threats. It also points to the rapid deterioration of European economies in the winter of 1946 to 1947 [1].

Those are the contemporary American assessments recorded by two official sources, so they reflect how US policymakers framed the problem rather than a neutral verdict. They are still essential to understanding why the program was proposed when it was.

What Marshall said at Harvard

On June 5, 1947, Secretary of State George C. Marshall spoke to the graduating class at Harvard University and called for a comprehensive program to rebuild Europe [1]. The National Archives reproduces the text. Marshall argued that the visible destruction of cities, factories, mines, and railroads had been correctly estimated, but that it was probably less serious than the dislocation of the whole fabric of the European economy [2].

He described a specific mechanism. Farmers normally grow food to exchange for the goods made in towns and cities. If urban industry cannot supply goods, such as machinery, fuel, and raw materials, farmers have no reason to sell for money they cannot spend, and they may withdraw fields from cultivation. Cities then run short of food and fuel, and governments spend scarce foreign money and credit buying necessities abroad, which drains funds needed for reconstruction. Marshall called this a vicious circle that threatened the division of labor on which modern civilization depends [2].

He also stated the American interest directly. It was logical, he said, for the United States to help restore normal economic health in the world, without which there could be no political stability and no assured peace. He declared that the policy was directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation, and chaos [2]. Those lines are quoted in many histories because they connect humanitarian and strategic motives in a single passage.

A plan drawn up by Europeans

One feature of the speech is easy to overlook. Marshall said that it would be neither fitting nor efficacious for the US government to draw up unilaterally a program to put Europe back on its feet. The initiative, he said, must come from Europe, with the American role consisting of friendly aid in drafting a joint program agreed to by a number, if not all, of the European nations [2]. He also warned that any assistance should provide a cure rather than a mere palliative, and should not come piecemeal as crises develop [2].

The speech did not offer open-ended help to everyone on any terms. Marshall said that any government willing to assist in recovery would find full cooperation from the United States, while any government that maneuvered to block the recovery of other countries could not expect help [2]. The State Department explains how this played out: participation by the Soviet Union and Eastern European nations was initially a possibility, but Soviet concern over potential US economic domination of its Eastern European satellites, together with Stalin's unwillingness to open the Soviet system to westerners, doomed the idea. As a result the plan was applied solely to Western Europe [1].

The State Department adds a political observation: it is unlikely that Congress would have funded the plan as generously as it did if aid had also gone to Soviet bloc Communist nations [1]. That is the department's historical judgment, not a documented vote count, but it shows that the geographic limits were shaped by both sides.

From speech to law

The path to legislation took less than a year. According to the National Archives, President Harry Truman sent Congress a message on December 19, 1947, following Marshall's ideas on aid to Europe. Congress overwhelmingly passed the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948, and Truman signed it on April 3, 1948 [2]. The State Department dates congressional passage to March 1948 [1].

The naming is slightly tangled, which is worth knowing when you read sources. The National Archives page describes the measure as the Economic Recovery Act of 1948 in its summary, but the transcript of the enrolled act shows that it may be cited as the Foreign Assistance Act of 1948, with Title I cited as the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948 [2]. The popular label, the Marshall Plan, named the program for the secretary of state who proposed it [2].

What the act said it was for

The enrolled text includes a statement of findings. Congress found that the existing situation in Europe endangered the establishment of a lasting peace, the general welfare and national interest of the United States, and the attainment of the objectives of the United Nations. It said that restoring principles of individual liberty, free institutions, and genuine independence in European countries rests largely on sound economic conditions, stable international economic relationships, and a healthy European economy independent of extraordinary outside assistance [2].

The text calls for a plan of European recovery open to all nations that cooperate in it, based on a strong production effort, expanded foreign trade, internal financial stability, and economic cooperation, including steps to maintain equitable exchange rates and progressively eliminate trade barriers. It also draws a comparison: mindful of the advantages the United States had enjoyed through a large domestic market without internal trade barriers, Congress believed similar advantages could accrue to the countries of Europe [2]. That is a notable statement of intent, because it ties recovery to integration among the recipient countries rather than aid alone.

The National Archives transcript omits many pages, so the excerpt supports only these points and not a complete description of how the aid was administered. One provision visible in the excerpt is outside Europe: a title concerning China, which authorized advances by the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and a joint commission on rural reconstruction in China [2]. The act was therefore a broader foreign assistance measure, with the European program as its central title.

How much money?

The two sources give slightly different figures, and the difference is instructive. The State Department says Congress approved funding that would eventually rise to over 12 billion dollars for rebuilding Western Europe [1]. The National Archives says that over the next four years Congress appropriated 13.3 billion dollars for European recovery [2]. The figures are not necessarily contradictory, since they may count different categories or time periods, but the sources do not explain the gap. A careful writer should therefore describe the total as roughly 12 to 13 billion dollars in US appropriations, and avoid false precision. Converting those sums to present-day values requires an inflation adjustment that neither source provides, so this article does not attempt it.

What the plan was meant to achieve

The National Archives lists several purposes for the United States: the aid provided markets for American goods, created reliable trading partners, and supported the development of stable democratic governments in Western Europe. The aid also provided capital and materials that enabled Europeans to rebuild the continent's economy [2]. The State Department says the plan generated a resurgence of European industrialization, brought extensive investment into the region, and stimulated the US economy by establishing markets for American goods [1].

It also made a political point at home. The National Archives notes that congressional approval signaled an extension of the bipartisanship of World War II into the postwar years [2]. Marshall himself had said that political passion and prejudice should have no part in the American public's understanding of the problem [2].

Where historians disagree

The State Department is notably cautious about the plan's measurable effect. It says economic historians have debated the precise impact of the Marshall Plan on Western Europe, but that these differing opinions do not detract from the fact that the program has been recognized as a great humanitarian effort [1]. For readers, the lesson is that claims such as the Marshall Plan single-handedly rebuilt Europe go beyond what these sources say. European countries were also rebuilding through their own work, and the plan was designed to be a joint program with European initiative [2].

The department also credits the plan with lasting institutional effects: it institutionalized and legitimized the concept of US foreign aid programs, which became an integral part of US foreign policy. It adds that Marshall became the only general ever to receive a Nobel Prize for peace [1]. Moscow, meanwhile, increasingly viewed the economic revival of Western Europe, especially West Germany, with suspicion [1].

Why it still matters

The Marshall Plan is often cited when governments debate foreign aid, and the sources show why it works as a case study. It combined a clear diagnosis of an economic problem, a requirement that recipients coordinate among themselves, and a mixture of humanitarian and self-interested arguments that Marshall made openly. It also shows the limits of any single explanation. Aid was shaped by Cold War rivalry, excluded the Soviet bloc, and produced debates among historians that remain unresolved.

Conclusion

The Marshall Plan began as a speech identifying a breakdown in Europe's economic circulation, became law in April 1948, and committed roughly 12 to 13 billion dollars of US funds over about four years. Its design asked Europeans to lead, its scope was limited to Western Europe, and its precise economic effect is still debated. Reading the primary text alongside an official summary gives a clearer picture than slogans do.

Sources

[1] US Department of State, Office of the Historian, Marshall Plan, 1948 (Milestones in the History of U.S. Foreign Relations, retired) - https://history.state.gov/milestones/1945-1952/marshall-plan

[2] US National Archives, Marshall Plan (1948) - https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/marshall-plan

title: How to Read a Nutrition Facts Label: FDA and NHS Tips
summary: How to read a nutrition facts label: check serving size first, use percent Daily Value, compare added sugars, and see how UK traffic-light labels differ.
seo: how to read a nutrition facts label, percent daily value, serving size, added sugars, food labels UK
author: knowledge blog
content:
Standing in a supermarket aisle with two similar products, most people glance at the front of the package and guess. The nutrition label on the back is designed to replace the guess with a quick comparison, but only if you know which numbers to read first. This article explains how to read a nutrition facts label using guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration and the UK National Health Service. It covers serving size, calories, the nutrients to limit and the nutrients to seek, the percent Daily Value, and how the UK system differs. It is general consumer information and not personal dietary advice; people with medical conditions or special dietary needs should ask a registered professional.

Start with the serving size

The FDA says the first thing to look at is the number of servings in the package and the serving size. Serving sizes are standardized so similar foods are easier to compare, and they are given in familiar units such as cups or pieces, followed by a metric amount. The agency stresses that the serving size reflects the amount people typically eat or drink and is not a recommendation of how much you should eat or drink [1].

All the amounts on the label, including calories, refer to that serving. The FDA's worked example is a frozen lasagna where one serving equals one cup. Eating two cups means two servings, which doubles the calories, the nutrient amounts, and the percent Daily Values [1]. In the example, one serving contains 280 calories, so a package holding four servings has 1,120 calories if eaten all at once [1].

This is the most common source of confusion. A product can look modest per serving while the whole package, which many people finish in one sitting, contains several servings. The FDA notes that for some products that could be eaten in one sitting or several, manufacturers provide dual-column labels showing amounts per serving and per package or unit. Its example is a bag of pretzels with three servings per container [1].

Calories: a measure of energy

The FDA explains that calories measure how much energy you get from a serving. To maintain a healthy body weight, it says, you should balance the calories you eat and drink with the calories your body uses. The 2,000 calories a day figure is a general guide used for nutrition advice, and your own needs may be higher or lower depending on age, sex, height, weight, and physical activity level [1]. The FDA points to MyPlate for an estimate of individual needs [1]. In practice, that means the 2,000 figure on the label is a reference point and not a target for any one person.

Nutrients to get less of

The FDA singles out three nutrients to limit: saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars. It says that Americans generally consume too much of them, and that eating too much saturated fat and sodium is associated with a higher risk of conditions such as cardiovascular disease and high blood pressure. Too many added sugars, it says, can make it hard to meet important nutrient needs while staying within calorie limits [1].

Total sugars and added sugars are not the same thing. Total sugars include sugars naturally present in foods such as milk and fruit as well as any added sugars. Added sugars include sugars added during processing, such as sucrose or dextrose, foods packaged as sweeteners such as table sugar, syrups and honey, and sugars from concentrated fruit or vegetable juices. The word includes before added sugars on the label shows that they are counted within the total [1]. The FDA's yogurt example has 7 grams of added sugars and 8 grams of naturally occurring sugars, for 15 grams in all [1]. Because there is no recommended daily total for sugars as a whole, the label has no percent Daily Value for total sugars [1].

Nutrients to get more of

The FDA names dietary fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium as nutrients that Americans generally do not get in recommended amounts. It says diets high in fiber can increase the frequency of bowel movements, lower blood glucose and cholesterol levels, and reduce calorie intake, while diets higher in vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium can reduce the risk of osteoporosis, anemia, and high blood pressure [1]. The practical advice is to use the label to support your own dietary needs, choosing foods higher in the nutrients you want more of and lower in those you want to limit [1].

What percent Daily Value means

The percent Daily Value, or %DV, is the part of the label that does the arithmetic for you. The Daily Values are reference amounts of nutrients to consume or not to exceed each day, and the %DV shows how much a serving of the food contributes to a total daily diet. The FDA says it puts all nutrients on the same scale for the day, from 0 to 100 percent, and that the column does not add up vertically to 100 percent [1].

The agency offers a simple guide: 5 percent DV or less of a nutrient per serving is low, and 20 percent DV or more is high [1]. Using it, the FDA's lasagna example with 37 percent DV for sodium is a high-sodium product, and eating two servings provides 74 percent, nearly three-quarters of a day's worth of sodium [1].

The FDA also lists the reference amounts that equal 100 percent DV on a 2,000 calorie diet. They are 20 grams of saturated fat, 2,300 milligrams of sodium, 28 grams of dietary fiber, 50 grams of added sugars, 20 micrograms of vitamin D, 1,300 milligrams of calcium, 18 milligrams of iron, and 4,700 milligrams of potassium. For saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars the goal is less than that amount, and for fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium the goal is at least that amount [1].

Three uses of the percent Daily Value

The FDA suggests several ways to use it. First, compare similar products, making sure the serving size is the same. Second, check claims such as light, low, or reduced by comparing the %DV in each product, with no need to memorize the definitions. Third, make trade-offs across the day: you do not have to give up a favorite food, but when a food is high in saturated fat you can balance it with lower-fat choices at other times and keep the day's total below 100 percent DV for nutrients to limit [1].

Nutrients without a percent Daily Value

Some items on the US label have no %DV. Trans fat has none because experts could not provide a reference value. The FDA says diets higher in trans fat are associated with higher LDL cholesterol and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, and that most uses of artificial trans fat in the US food supply were phased out as of 2018 [1]. Protein lists a %DV only in specific situations, such as when a claim like high in protein is made or when the product is for infants and children under 4 [1]. Total sugars, as noted above, also have none [1].

A special case concerns single-ingredient sugars such as pure honey or maple syrup. They are not required to state grams of added sugars but must still show the percent Daily Value for added sugars, so that the label does not suggest sugar was added and still informs you how a serving contributes to your daily intake [1].

How the UK system differs

The NHS explains that all pre-packed foods in the UK carry a nutrition information label on the back or side that must include energy in kilojoules and kilocalories, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, and salt, and may include other nutrients such as fibre. The information is provided per 100 grams or per 100 millilitres, and sometimes per portion [2]. The per-100-gram basis is a useful contrast with the US approach, because it makes products comparable regardless of how large each manufacturer's serving is.

The NHS provides thresholds for what counts as high or low per 100 grams. For total fat, high is more than 17.5 grams and low is 3 grams or less. For saturated fat, high is more than 5 grams and low is 1.5 grams or less. For total sugars, high is more than 22.5 grams and low is 5 grams or less. For salt, high is more than 1.5 grams and low is 0.3 grams or less, which corresponds to 0.6 and 0.1 grams of sodium. Different criteria apply to drinks [2]. Note that salt and sodium are not interchangeable: the US label lists sodium, while UK labels list salt, so comparing numbers across countries requires care.

Front-of-pack labels and colors

Many UK supermarkets and manufacturers also display energy, fat, saturated fat, sugars, and salt on the front of the pack. Some use red, amber, and green colors: red means high, amber medium, and green low. The NHS says that a product that is all or mostly green is generally a healthier choice, amber foods can be eaten most of the time, and any red means the food is high in fat, saturated fat, salt, or sugars and should be eaten less often and in small amounts [2]. It cautions that the manufacturer's idea of a portion may differ from yours [2].

The ingredients list as a second check

The NHS adds that ingredients must be listed in descending order of weight, so the main ingredients come first, and allergens must be highlighted in bold. If the first few items are high-fat ingredients such as cream, butter, or oil, the food is likely to be high in fat [2]. This check complements the numbers, since it shows what the product is made of and not only how much of each nutrient it holds.

A quick routine for shopping

Combining the two sources gives a short routine. Check the serving size, and decide how many servings you will actually eat. Look at calories for that amount. Scan saturated fat, sodium or salt, and added sugars, using 5 percent DV or less as low and 20 percent or more as high in the US, or the per-100-gram thresholds and colors in the UK. When comparing two products, make sure the serving basis is the same. Finally, read the first few ingredients. This routine is a synthesis of the cited guidance rather than an official procedure, and the thresholds apply to the packaged foods described, not to fresh produce or whole diets.

Limits of the label

A label describes a product, not a diet. The FDA stresses that you can make dietary trade-offs across the day instead of treating any one food as forbidden [1], and the NHS ties labels to the goal of eating a balanced diet [2]. Labels also cannot tell you your personal needs, which depend on age, activity, health, and other factors [1].

Conclusion

Reading a nutrition label comes down to a few habits: identify the serving size, convert the numbers to what you actually eat, use the percent Daily Value or the UK high and low thresholds to judge each nutrient, and compare products on equal terms. The US and UK systems use different formats but share the aim of letting shoppers decide quickly and with evidence.

Sources

[1] US Food and Drug Administration, How to Understand and Use the Nutrition Facts Label - https://www.fda.gov/food/nutrition-facts-label/how-understand-and-use-nutrition-facts-label

[2] National Health Service (UK), Food labels - https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/food-guidelines-and-food-labels/how-to-read-food-labels/

title: How DNS Works: Domain Names, Resolvers, and Name Servers
summary: How DNS works: learn how domain names become IP addresses through resolvers, name servers, zones, and caching, and why the system was designed this way.
seo: how DNS works, domain name system explained, DNS resolver and name server, what is a DNS zone
author: knowledge blog
content:
Every time you type a website name into a browser, a quiet lookup happens before a single page element loads. Your device needs a numeric Internet Protocol (IP) address to reach a server, but people remember names far better than numbers. The Domain Name System, usually shortened to DNS, is the global service that connects the two. This article explains how DNS works, what its main parts do, and why it was built as a distributed system rather than a single directory.

The problem DNS was built to solve

The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) describes the basic job simply: every computer on the Internet has a unique address, much like a telephone number, and the DNS lets people use a familiar string of letters, a domain name, instead of that numeric address. ICANN's own example is that you can type icann.org rather than a numeric address that begins 192.0 [1]. The exact number behind any name can change over time, so treat any address quoted in an article as an illustration rather than a permanent fact.

The history matters because it explains the design. According to RFC 1034, the 1987 specification that introduced the concepts behind DNS, host names and addresses were once kept in a single file called HOSTS.TXT, maintained by the Network Information Center and copied by every host on the network [2]. The document points out that the bandwidth needed to distribute each new version grew roughly with the square of the number of hosts, and that organizations had to wait for the central file to change before their own new names became visible [2]. As networks grew from a few timeshared machines to many local networks of workstations, a single master list stopped scaling.

The replacement was a hierarchical, distributed database. RFC 1034 lists several design goals, including a consistent name space that does not embed network addresses or routes in the names, a database spread across many servers with local caching for speed, and a system that is useful for more than one application [2].

A tree of names

DNS organizes names as a tree. RFC 1034 explains that each node in the tree has a label of zero to 63 octets, and that the single empty label is reserved for the root [2]. A full domain name is the list of labels on the path from a node up to the root, written from the most specific label on the left to the least specific on the right [2]. In www.example.org, the label www is the most specific, example sits above it, and org sits above that, just below the root.

The specification adds a few details that are easy to miss. A complete name technically ends with a dot that stands for the root, so www.example.org. is the absolute form, while a name written without the trailing dot is often treated as relative and completed by local software [2]. The total length of a name is limited to 255 octets [2]. Name comparison is case-insensitive, so WWW.Example.ORG and www.example.org refer to the same place, although the case a person typed is preserved [2]. And a domain is simply the part of the tree at or below a given name, which is why www.example.org is a subdomain of example.org and of org [2].

Three components: names, name servers, and resolvers

RFC 1034 divides the system into three major components [2]. The first is the domain name space and its resource records, the data attached to names. Each record is tagged with a type and a class, which lets a query ask for one kind of information, such as a host address, rather than everything stored under a name [2]. The same mechanism lets a name carry other data, such as mail routing information, which is why DNS is useful beyond web browsing.

The second component is the name server. A name server holds information about part of the tree and pointers that lead toward other parts. When a server has complete information for a part of the name space, it is said to be an authority for it. Authoritative data is organized into units called zones, and a zone can be copied automatically to several servers so that more than one machine can answer for it [2]. This is why organizations are encouraged to run redundant name servers: if one fails, another can still answer.

The third component is the resolver. A resolver is the program that extracts information from name servers on behalf of a client. According to RFC 1034, it must be able to reach at least one name server and either use that server's information to answer directly or follow referrals to other name servers [2]. On a typical computer, the resolver is a system routine that applications call, so a web browser does not need to speak the DNS protocol itself [2].

A lookup, step by step

Because no single server knows everything, a lookup can involve several hops. The specification describes two general ways to handle a query that a server cannot answer itself. In the recursive approach, the first server pursues the answer at other servers on behalf of the client. In the iterative approach, the server refers the client to another server and lets the client continue the search [2]. RFC 1034 says implementations are required to support the iterative approach and may offer the recursive approach as an option [2].

Putting that together, a simplified lookup for www.example.org looks like this. Your application asks the local resolver. The resolver asks a server that knows about the root of the tree, which refers it to servers responsible for org. Those servers refer it to the servers responsible for example.org, and one of those authoritative servers returns the address record for www. The resolver hands the answer back to your application, which connects to the address. In practice many home and office networks forward questions to a shared resolving service, so only that service performs the longer chain of questions. That arrangement is a deployment choice rather than part of the core naming design, and it is one reason different networks can give different speeds for the same lookup.

Caching and why changes take time

Because the same questions are asked constantly, DNS relies heavily on caching. The RFC's design goals state that the database must be distributed with local caching to improve performance [2]. It also describes how freshness is handled: the party that owns the data sets a timeout, and whoever holds a copy is responsible for refreshing it when the timeout expires [2]. The document notes that the source of the data should control the tradeoff between the cost of getting data, the speed of updates, and the accuracy of caches [2].

This is the reason a website owner who changes the address behind a name may see the change appear at different times for different people. The specification says plainly that access to information is considered more critical than instantaneous updates, so updates percolate out through the system instead of reaching every copy at once [2]. When updates are unavailable because of a network or host failure, the usual course is to keep believing the old information while continuing to try to update it [2]. For a reader, the practical lesson is that a recent DNS change is not necessarily wrong or broken if some devices still see the old answer for a while.

Who controls what

The design also divides responsibility. RFC 1034 describes administrators who define zone boundaries, maintain the master files from which name servers load their data, and set the refresh policies they want [2]. The DNS in turn provides standard record formats, standard query methods, and standard ways for name servers to refresh data from one another [2]. The result is that the owner of a domain controls the records under it without needing a central authority to approve each change, while the shared tree keeps names consistent across the whole Internet.

The specification also makes a point about what DNS is not. It does not require a particular tree structure or rules for choosing labels, so the same machinery can hold information for many different purposes [2]. The same document gives an example of mailbox names being mapped into domain names, with the part before the at sign turned into a single label, which shows how a general naming service can support applications that were not part of the original host-lookup idea [2].

Practical takeaways

Understanding the basic model makes common problems easier to reason about. If a site cannot be reached by name but works by numeric address, the naming layer is the first suspect. If a recent change shows for some people and not others, cached answers that have not yet expired are a likely explanation. If you manage a domain, having more than one authoritative name server follows the redundancy the specification recommends [2]. And because DNS was designed as a general naming system, a single domain can hold several kinds of records, so it is worth knowing which type a service actually asks for.

A caution is also in order. RFC 1034 is a foundational document from 1987, and it warns readers not to depend on its example values being current [2]. DNS has been extended since then, and modern deployments add features, such as security extensions and encrypted transports, that this early specification does not describe. The concepts of a hierarchy, zones, authority, resolvers, and caching remain the right starting point, but anyone configuring a real system should consult current documentation from their provider or registry.

Conclusion

DNS turns readable names into the numbers computers need by splitting the work among a hierarchy of authoritative name servers and resolvers that cache what they learn. That distributed design emerged because a single shared file could not keep up with a growing network [2]. Seeing a domain name as a path through a tree, answered by whichever server is responsible for that branch, explains both why the system scales and why changes take time to spread.

Sources

[1] ICANN, ICANN Acronyms and Terms: Domain Name System (DNS) - https://www.icann.org/en/icann-acronyms-and-terms/domain-name-system-en

[2] P. Mockapetris, IETF RFC 1034, Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities (November 1987) - https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1034

title: How Wetlands Work: Water Filtering, Flood Control, Habitat
summary: How wetlands work: see how marshes, swamps, and bogs filter water, slow floods, store carbon, and support wildlife, and why losing them matters.
seo: how wetlands work, benefits of wetlands, wetlands water filtration, why wetlands are important
author: knowledge blog
content:
For much of history, wetlands were treated as wasteland to be drained, filled, or used as dumping grounds. Today, public agencies describe them very differently: as hardworking natural systems that clean water, soften floods, and support an unusual share of wildlife. This article explains what wetlands are, how their main functions work, and what the evidence from US agencies says about why they matter.

What counts as a wetland

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) defines wetlands as areas where water covers the soil, or is present at or near the surface, all year or for varying periods during the year, including during the growing season [1]. Two features follow from that. The water determines how the soil develops and which plants and animals can live there, and the prolonged wetness favors specially adapted plants and characteristic wetland soils [1]. For regulatory purposes under the Clean Water Act, wetlands generally include swamps, marshes, bogs, and similar areas [1].

Wetlands vary widely with soils, topography, climate, water chemistry, and vegetation, and they occur from the tundra to the tropics on every continent except Antarctica [1]. EPA recognizes two broad groups: coastal or tidal wetlands and inland or non-tidal wetlands [1]. Coastal types include tidal salt marshes and the mangrove swamps of warm climates, while inland types include floodplain wetlands along rivers, isolated depressions such as prairie potholes, lake margins, vernal pools, and bogs [1]. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) uses a different scheme with five types: marine, estuarine, riverine, lacustrine, and palustrine [3]. The two systems are not in conflict. They are simply different ways to classify a very diverse set of places.

Because many wetlands are seasonal, a site can look dry for part of the year and still qualify. EPA notes that vernal pools, which can appear dry for long stretches, often provide critical habitat for wildlife that breeds only there [1]. A wetland is therefore defined by its hydrology, soils, and vegetation over time, not by whether you see standing water on a given day.

How wetlands filter water

The water-quality function is among the best known. The National Park Service (NPS) describes wetlands as natural purifiers that filter sediment and absorb many pollutants in surface water, and says that in some systems this cleansing can also improve groundwater supplies [4]. NOAA adds that wetlands absorb excess nutrients, sediments, and other pollutants before they reach rivers, lakes, and other bodies of water [3].

The general idea can be understood without much chemistry. Water that enters a wetland usually slows down. Dense vegetation and shallow flow give suspended particles time to settle, and the plants, soil, and microbes that live there take up or transform dissolved substances. EPA describes wetland microbes, plants, and wildlife as part of the global cycles of water, nitrogen, and sulfur [2], which is consistent with wetlands acting as a processing zone for nutrients. How much a particular wetland removes depends on its size, its position in the landscape, how much water flows through it, and what the water carries, so the agencies' statements describe a typical function rather than a guaranteed result for every site.

Flood control and drought buffering

EPA compares wetlands to natural sponges that trap and slowly release surface water, rain, snowmelt, groundwater, and floodwater [2].
