Trees, root mats, and other vegetation slow the speed of floodwaters and spread them across the floodplain. That combined storage acts as a brake that lowers flood peaks and reduces erosion [2]. EPA also points out that wetlands within and downstream of urban areas are especially valuable because they counteract the faster, larger runoff from pavement and buildings [2].

The same storage that helps during storms can matter in dry periods. NPS says wetlands along rivers and streams absorb energy and store water during storms, reducing downstream flood damage and the risk of flash floods, and that the slow release of stored water can help keep streams flowing during drought [4]. On coasts, NPS notes that mangrove forests and salt marshes help blunt the force of major storms, reducing flooding, erosion, and property damage [4].

EPA offers one concrete illustration of what loss can mean. It reports that the bottomland hardwood and riparian wetlands along the Mississippi River once stored at least 60 days of floodwater, but now store only about 12 days because most have been filled or drained [2]. The agency adds that preserving and restoring wetlands, together with other water retention, can often provide flood control that would otherwise require expensive dredging and levees [2]. That does not mean wetlands replace engineered defenses everywhere. It means they can be a cost-effective part of a broader flood plan.

Habitat and biological productivity

Wetlands are among the most productive ecosystems in the world, comparable to rain forests and coral reefs, according to EPA [2]. The agency explains why: the combination of shallow water, abundant nutrients, and high plant growth supports organisms at the base of the food web. Dead leaves and stems break down into small organic particles called detritus, which feeds insects, shellfish, and small fish that in turn feed larger animals [2]. EPA's phrase for this is a biological supermarket [2].

The numbers cited by the agencies are striking, but they should be read carefully. EPA states that more than one-third of threatened and endangered species in the United States live only in wetlands, and nearly half use wetlands at some point in their lives [2]. NPS uses a slightly different framing, saying that about one-third of listed plants and animals depend on wetlands for survival [4]. The two statements agree on the general scale even though they are worded differently. NPS also says that nearly 7,000 plant species live in US wetlands, that prairie potholes provide breeding grounds for over 50 percent of North American waterfowl, and that between 60 and 90 percent of US commercial fisheries depend on wetlands [4]. These figures come from US contexts and should not be assumed to apply unchanged to other countries.

The productivity of some wetlands is also remarkable in a farming comparison. NPS reports that a stand of cordgrass in a salt marsh can produce more plant material and store more energy per acre than any agricultural crop except cultivated sugar cane [4]. Nutrients and plant material flushed from such wetlands during storms can feed estuaries and other downstream ecosystems [4].

Carbon and climate

EPA notes that scientists now recognize an additional atmospheric function: wetlands store carbon in their plants and soils rather than releasing it to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, which helps moderate global climate conditions [2]. NPS likewise lists carbon sequestration among the services wetlands provide [4]. The sources describe this as a benefit of intact wetlands. Neither page claims that wetlands alone can offset human emissions, and that would be an overreach. The more defensible reading is that keeping existing wetlands intact avoids releasing what they have stored, and restoring degraded ones can restore some of the function.

What has been lost

The benefits are easier to value once the scale of past loss is clear. NPS cites a 1990 study published by the US Fish and Wildlife Service which found that more than half of the 221 million acres of wetlands that existed in the lower 48 states in the late 1700s had been destroyed [4]. It describes a time when draining and filling were common practice, which is partly why protection and restoration are now seen as worthwhile investments [4]. The figure is a historical estimate from one study, not a measure of current conditions, so readers who need today's numbers should consult recent national status reports.

Practical takeaways for readers

You do not need to own a marsh to benefit from wetlands or to help them. Knowing that wetlands can be seasonal helps explain why a field that is dry in August may still be protected and still matter. Supporting local watershed groups, following local rules about development near wet areas, and keeping fertilizers and chemicals away from storm drains reduce the load that downstream wetlands must handle. EPA emphasizes that a wetland's functions depend on its relationships with other ecosystems in the watershed, the area from which water and dissolved materials drain to a common low point [2]. That means actions upstream influence what a wetland can do.

A balanced view also acknowledges limits. Wetlands differ in size and condition, and a degraded or heavily loaded one may not perform the functions described in general agency summaries. Estimates of flood storage or pollutant removal for a specific place require local study.

Conclusion

Wetlands work by holding water long enough for sediment to settle, plants and microbes to process nutrients, and floods to spread out and slow down, all while supplying food and shelter to a wide range of species. US agencies describe them as water purifiers, flood buffers, carbon stores, and habitat [1][2][3][4]. The historical record of drainage shows that these services are easy to lose and hard to replace, which is the practical case for protecting and restoring them.

Sources

[1] US Environmental Protection Agency, What is a Wetland? - https://www.epa.gov/wetlands/what-wetland

[2] US Environmental Protection Agency, Why are Wetlands Important? - https://www.epa.gov/wetlands/why-are-wetlands-important

[3] National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, What is a wetland? - https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/wetland.html

[4] National Park Service, Why are Wetlands Important? - https://www.nps.gov/subjects/wetlands/why.htm

title: Moon Phases Explained: Why the Moon Changes Shape Each Month
summary: Moon phases explained: learn why the Moon seems to change shape over about 29.5 days, how rise and set times shift, and what earthshine and libration are.
seo: moon phases explained, why does the moon change shape, lunar cycle 29.5 days, waxing and waning moon
author: knowledge blog
content:
The Moon seems to grow from nothing to a bright disc and back again every month. It is natural to assume the Moon itself is changing, or that Earth's shadow is sweeping across it. Neither is the case. This article explains moon phases using NASA's educational material and the astronomy reference site timeanddate.com, covers how to read the eight phases, and clears up some common confusion about moonrise times, half Moons, and the faint glow of a dark Moon.

The core idea: half the Moon is always lit

According to NASA, the Moon does not make its own light. Moonlight is reflected sunlight, and the Sun is the only object in our solar system that shines with its own light [1]. NASA also stresses that the Sun always illuminates half of the Moon while the other half stays dark, just as Earth has a day side and a night side [1]. Timeanddate.com makes the same point: half of the Moon's surface is always lit by sunlight, and as the Moon orbits Earth it changes how much of the lit half we can see [2].

That is the whole mechanism. The phases are a matter of viewing angle. The Moon travels around Earth, and from our position we see the lit half from different directions over the month. When the lit half faces away from us we see little or nothing. When it faces us we see a full disc. In between we see partial shapes. The amount of Moon that is lit never changes. Only the part of it that points toward us changes.

The eight phases in order

NASA lists the eight lunar phases in order as new Moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full Moon, waning gibbous, third quarter (also called last quarter), and waning crescent. The cycle repeats about every 29.5 days [1]. Timeanddate.com uses the same eight names and divides them into four primary phases, which happen at a specific moment, and four intermediate phases, which fill the time between those moments [2]. The four primary phases are new Moon, first quarter, full Moon, and third quarter.

Waxing means the visible lit portion is growing. Waning means it is shrinking. Crescent describes less than half of the visible disc lit, and gibbous describes more than half lit. Those four words, combined with new, quarter, and full, are enough to name every stage.

New Moon. NASA calls this the invisible phase. The illuminated side faces the Sun and the dark side faces Earth, and the Moon sits in about the same part of the sky as the Sun, rising and setting with it [1]. Timeanddate.com describes the Moon as between the Sun and Earth, with moonrise near sunrise [2]. One subtle point from NASA is that the Moon does not usually pass directly between Earth and the Sun at this phase, because its orbit is inclined. It only passes near the Sun from our perspective [1].

Waxing crescent. A thin sliver appears as the Moon's orbit carries more of its day side into view. NASA notes that it grows daily and that the Moon rises a little later each day [1]. For observers in the Northern Hemisphere, timeanddate.com says the lit part appears on the right side, while in the Southern Hemisphere it appears on the left [2].

First quarter. The Moon is a quarter of the way through its journey, and we see half of its lit side. NASA points out that people casually call this a half Moon, but what we really see is half of the illuminated half [1]. It rises around midday and sets around the middle of the night, so it is high in the sky in the evening and good for viewing [1].

Waxing gibbous. Most of the day side is now in view, and the Moon looks brighter [1]. Moonrise happens in the afternoon [2].

Full Moon. The Moon is opposite the Sun as seen from Earth, so the whole day side faces us. NASA says a full Moon rises around sunset and sets around sunrise, and appears full for a couple of days [1]. Timeanddate.com adds that the Moon and Sun are on opposite sides of Earth at this time [2].

Waning gibbous, third quarter, and waning crescent. After full, the lit side appears to shrink, although NASA clarifies that the Moon's orbit is simply carrying it out of view from our perspective [1]. It rises later each night. A third quarter Moon rises around the middle of the night and sets around midday [1]. In the Northern Hemisphere, the lit part now appears on the left side [2]. The waning crescent is the thin curve that remains as the Moon nears the point where its day side faces the Sun again [1].

Why rise and set times shift

A practical way to use the phase is to predict when the Moon is up. NASA says moonrise and moonset times shift with the phases: a full Moon rises at sunset, and a new Moon is up all day [1]. Timeanddate.com's summary gives the same pattern, with moonrise near midday for the first quarter Moon and near midnight for the third quarter [2]. This is why a Moon visible in the afternoon sky is not unusual. NASA notes that the Moon is often visible during the day as a faint, pale presence, depending on the phase and time [1]. If you see a bright, nearly half-lit Moon in the blue afternoon sky, you are probably looking at a waxing Moon around first quarter.

Phases are not eclipses

A common mistake is to blame Earth's shadow for the phases. Eclipses are a different event with a different cause. Timeanddate.com explains that if the Moon's path crosses the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun, called the ecliptic, while the Sun, Moon, and Earth are lined up at new Moon, a solar eclipse occurs somewhere in the world. If the same crossing happens while the three are aligned at full Moon, a lunar eclipse occurs on the night side of Earth [2]. Because the Moon's orbit is tilted, the alignment usually does not cross the plane, which is why we do not have an eclipse every month. NASA's remark that the new Moon usually does not pass directly between Earth and the Sun reflects the same geometry [1].

Earthshine: the dim glow on a dark Moon

During a crescent phase, you can sometimes see the unlit part of the Moon glowing faintly. NASA explains that this effect, called earthshine, is sunlight reflecting off Earth's surface onto the Moon's near side [1]. At that point in the orbit, Earth would look nearly full from the Moon, so the light it reflects is bright enough to dimly illuminate the dark area [1]. Timeanddate.com also names the crescent phases as a good time to see earthshine [2]. This gives a neat way to remember how the system works: when the Moon shows a thin crescent to us, Earth is showing most of its lit face to the Moon.

Libration: the wobbling Moon

Phases are not the only change in the Moon's appearance over a month. NASA describes libration as the apparent twisting, nodding, and rolling that lets observers see slightly more than half of the Moon's surface over time [1]. There are three main causes. Because the Moon's orbit is not a perfect circle, its distance and orbital speed vary, while its rotation rate stays constant, which produces libration in longitude and lets us see a little more of the eastern or western side [1]. The roughly 5 degree tilt of the Moon's orbit produces libration in latitude, an apparent nodding that reveals a bit more of the northern or southern regions [1]. Finally, Earth's 23.5 degree axial tilt creates an apparent metronome-like tilt as we observe from a tilted platform [1]. For casual observers, libration is subtle, but it explains why careful photographs taken in different weeks show slightly different edges of the same Moon.

How to observe the cycle yourself

You can check this explanation without equipment. On a clear evening, note the Moon's shape and where it sits relative to the Sun's position near the horizon. A thin crescent will be close to where the Sun set. A first quarter Moon will be high in the south or overhead in the evening in many northern locations. A full Moon will rise as the Sun sets. Returning at the same time each night for a week shows the Moon rising later and shifting eastward, which matches NASA's remark that the waxing Moon rises later each day [1]. Remember that the left and right orientation of the lit portion depends on your hemisphere [2].

Conclusion

Moon phases come from geometry, not from a changing Moon or Earth's shadow. Half of the Moon is always lit; the Moon's orbit, which repeats about every 29.5 days, changes how much of that lit half we see [1][2]. Once you know the order of the eight phases, you can estimate when the Moon rises and sets, understand why daytime Moons are normal, and recognize extras such as earthshine and libration that add detail to the monthly cycle.

Sources

[1] NASA Science, Moon Phases - https://science.nasa.gov/moon/moon-phases/

[2] timeanddate.com, Moon Phases: Moon Phases in Order - https://www.timeanddate.com/astronomy/moon/phases.html
